title: Child support
intro: This guide explains, in general terms, what Ontario’s Family Law Act, the federal Divorce Act and the child support guidelines say about child support and how the amount is worked out. It does not calculate any amount and does not say what any particular person would pay or receive.

sections.heading: The duty to support a child under the Family Law Act
paragraphs: Ontario’s Family Law Act says “Every parent has an obligation to provide support, to the extent that the parent is capable of doing so, for his or her unmarried child who,” is a minor, is enrolled in a full-time program of education, or is unable by reason of illness, disability or other cause to withdraw from parental care. The obligation “does not extend to a child who is sixteen years of age or older and has withdrawn from parental control.” (Family Law Act, s. 31 (1), (2))
The obligation does not extend to a child “who is sixteen years of age or older and has withdrawn from parental control.” (Family Law Act, s. 31 (2))

“A court may, on application, order a person to provide support for his or her dependants and determine the amount of support.” A dependant is “a person to whom another has an obligation to provide support under this Part”. The application may be made by “the dependant or the dependant’s parent”, and in some cases by an agency that provides social assistance or disability support for the dependant. (Family Law Act, ss. 29, 33 (1)-(3))

An order for the support of a child should “recognize that each parent has an obligation to provide support for the child” and apportion the obligation according to the child support guidelines. A court making the order “shall do so in accordance with the child support guidelines.” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (7), (11))

The Act allows a different amount in two situations. The first is where special provisions in an order or written agreement benefit the child and the guidelines amount would be “inequitable given those special provisions”; the court records its reasons. The second is on the consent of both parents, where “reasonable arrangements have been made for the support of the child” and, if support for the child is payable out of public money, the arrangements do not provide for less than the guidelines amount. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (12)-(14))

When a divorce proceeding is started under the Divorce Act, a support application under this Part of the Family Law Act that has not been adjudicated “is stayed, unless the court orders otherwise.” (Family Law Act, s. 36 (1))

sections.heading: Child support under the Divorce Act
paragraphs: Under the federal Divorce Act, “A court of competent jurisdiction may, on application by either or both spouses, make an order requiring a spouse to pay for the support of any or all children of the marriage.” The court may also make an interim order while the application is pending. (Divorce Act, s. 15.1 (1), (2))

The court makes the order “in accordance with the applicable guidelines.” It may award a different amount where special provisions benefit the child and the guidelines amount would be inequitable, or on the consent of both spouses if “reasonable arrangements have been made for the support of the child”. (Divorce Act, s. 15.1 (3), (5), (7))

Arrangements are not unreasonable “solely because the amount of support agreed to is not the same as the amount that would otherwise have been determined in accordance with the applicable guidelines.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.1 (8))
Where a court is considering applications for both child support and spousal support, “the court shall give priority to child support in determining the applications.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.3 (1))

sections.heading: Which guidelines and which table
paragraphs: The Divorce Act defines “applicable guidelines”. If both spouses habitually reside in the same province at the time the application is made and that province has been designated by an order under subsection 2 (5), they are “the laws of the province specified in the order”. Otherwise (“in any other case”), they are the Federal Child Support Guidelines. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1), (5))
This site does not yet have a source on disk that says whether Ontario has been designated under that subsection. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (5))

Ontario’s regulation covers both kinds of case. In it, “child” means a dependant under the Family Law Act or, “in cases where the Divorce Act (Canada) applies, a child of the marriage under that Act”. In a Divorce Act case, “spouse” means “either of two persons who are married to each other and includes a former spouse”. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 2 (1))

Under the Ontario regulation, the “table” is a table in the Federal Child Support Guidelines. If the parent or spouse against whom the order is sought ordinarily resides in Ontario at the time of the application, it is “the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for Ontario”; if elsewhere in Canada, the table for that province or territory. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 2 (1), (1.1))

The Ontario regulation has further rules for a change of residence since the application, a move expected in the near future, and a parent or spouse who resides outside Canada or whose residence is unknown. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 2 (1))

The Federal Child Support Guidelines also choose the applicable table by where the spouse against whom the order is sought habitually resides, with rules for a change of province, a move expected in the near future, and a spouse who resides outside Canada or whose residence is unknown. (Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 3 (3))

sections.heading: The basic amount: the table amount
paragraphs: Unless the guidelines provide otherwise, the amount for children under the age of majority is “the amount set out in the applicable table, according to the number of children under the age of majority to whom the order relates and the income of the parent or spouse against whom the order is sought”, plus any amount under section 7. The federal wording is the same except that it refers only to the spouse. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 3 (1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 3 (1))

For a child who is the age of majority or over, the amount is found by applying the guidelines as if the child were under that age, or, if the court considers that inappropriate, the amount it considers appropriate “having regard to the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of the child and the financial ability of each parent or spouse to contribute to the support of the child.” (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 3 (2))

Where the income of the person against whom the order is sought is over $150,000, the amount is the section 3 amount or, if the court considers that inappropriate, the table amount on the first $150,000 plus an amount the court considers appropriate on the balance, plus any section 7 amount. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 4; Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 4)

Where medical or dental insurance for the child is available to either parent or spouse “through his or her employer or otherwise at a reasonable rate, the court may order that coverage be acquired or continued.” (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 6; Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 6)

This guide does not calculate any amount. The guidelines say that an order must include, among other things, the income of any parent or spouse whose income is used and the amount determined under the table. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 13; Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 13)

sections.heading: Special or extraordinary expenses
paragraphs: On request, the court may provide for an amount to cover all or part of certain expenses, “taking into account the necessity of the expense in relation to the child’s best interests and the reasonableness of the expense in relation to the means of the parents or spouses and those of the child”, and to the spending pattern during cohabitation. The federal wording refers to “the family’s spending pattern prior to the separation”. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 7 (1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 7 (1))

The listed expenses are: child care expenses related to the employment, illness, disability or education or training for employment of the parent or spouse with the majority of parenting time; the child’s portion of medical and dental insurance premiums; health-related expenses “that exceed insurance reimbursement by at least $100 annually”; extraordinary expenses for primary or secondary school or other educational programs meeting the child’s particular needs; post-secondary education expenses; and extraordinary expenses for extracurricular activities. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 7 (1))

For school and extracurricular expenses, “extraordinary expenses” means expenses that exceed what the requesting parent or spouse can reasonably cover, taking into account their income and the table amount they would receive (or the amount the court has otherwise determined is appropriate). (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 7 (1.1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 7 (1.1))

Where that does not apply, the court considers the amount of the expense relative to the requesting person’s income, the nature and number of programs and activities, any special needs and talents of the child, the overall cost, and other similar factors. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 7 (1.1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 7 (1.1))

“The guiding principle” is that the expense “is shared by the parents or spouses in proportion to their respective incomes after deducting from the expense, the contribution, if any, from the child.” The court takes into account subsidies, benefits and income tax deductions or credits relating to the expense, and any eligibility to claim them, but not any universal child care benefit or eligibility to claim it. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 7 (2)-(4))

sections.heading: Split and shared parenting time
paragraphs: In the guidelines, “majority of parenting time” means “a period of time that is more than 60 per cent of parenting time over the course of a year”. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 2 (1))

Split parenting time: if there are two or more children and each parent or spouse has the majority of parenting time with one or more of them, the amount is “the difference between the amount that each parent or spouse would otherwise pay if such an order were sought against each of the parents or spouses.” The federal guidelines say the same thing in slightly different words. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 8; Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 8)

Shared parenting time: where each parent or spouse exercises parenting time “for not less than 40 per cent of the time over the course of a year”, the amount is determined by taking into account the table amounts for each of them, “the increased costs of shared parenting time arrangements”, and the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of each of them and of the child. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 9; Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 9)

sections.heading: Undue hardship
paragraphs: On the application of either spouse (or, under the Ontario regulation, an applicant under section 33 of the Family Law Act), a court may award a different amount from the amount under sections 3 to 5, 8 or 9 “if the court finds that the parent or spouse making the request, or a child in respect of whom the request is made, would otherwise suffer undue hardship.” (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 10 (1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 10 (1))

Listed circumstances that may cause undue hardship include an “unusually high level of debts reasonably incurred” to support the family during cohabitation or to earn a living; “unusually high expenses in relation to exercising parenting time with respect to a child”; a legal duty under a judgment, order or written separation agreement to support any person; and a legal duty to support other children, or a person unable to obtain the necessaries of life due to illness or disability. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 10 (2))

Even if undue hardship is found, the application “must be denied” if the court is of the opinion that the household of the person claiming undue hardship would, after child support is determined under sections 3 to 5, 8 or 9, have a higher standard of living than the other household. The court may use the test in Schedule II to compare. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 10 (3), (4); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 10 (3), (4))

Where the court orders a different amount because of undue hardship, it “must record its reasons for doing so.” (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 10 (6); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 10 (6))

sections.heading: How income is determined
paragraphs: Income is determined using the sources of income under the heading “Total income” in the T1 General form issued by the Canada Revenue Agency, adjusted under Schedule III, subject to sections 17 to 20. If both agree in writing on a person’s income, the court may use that amount if it is reasonable given the income information provided. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, ss. 15, 16; Federal Child Support Guidelines, ss. 15, 16)

If the section 16 figure “would not be the fairest determination of that income”, the court may look at income over the last three years. Special rules apply to a shareholder, director or officer of a corporation. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, ss. 17 (1), 18 (1))

“The court may impute such amount of income to a parent or spouse as it considers appropriate in the circumstances”. Listed circumstances include being intentionally under-employed or unemployed (with exceptions for a child’s needs or the person’s reasonable educational or health needs), income diverted, and having “failed to provide income information when under a legal obligation to do so”. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 19 (1))

An applicant whose income information is necessary to determine the amount includes with the application income tax returns and notices of assessment and reassessment “for each of the three most recent taxation years”, and other listed documents. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 21 (1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 21 (1))

A person served with the application whose income information is necessary must provide those documents to the court and the other party “within 30 days after the application is served” if they reside in Canada or the United States, or within 60 days if they reside elsewhere, or another time the court specifies. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 21 (2); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 21 (2))

sections.heading: Changing a child support order
paragraphs: Where the amount includes a table determination, a change of circumstances for a variation includes “any change in circumstances that would result in a different order for the support of a child or any provision thereof.” Where it does not, it includes “any change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances of either parent or spouse or of any child who is entitled to support.” (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 14)

The Federal Child Support Guidelines set out the same circumstances for varying a child support order under the Divorce Act, and the guidelines also apply to interim orders and to orders varying a child support order. (Federal Child Support Guidelines, ss. 2 (4), 14)
